A Square-Root Factor of the Penalty

Source: R/augmented.R
penalty_sqrt.Rd

Returns \(C\) with \(C'C = S(\theta)\), the block-diagonal penalty Hessian, omitting the rows that correspond to its null space.

Usage

penalty_sqrt(S)

Arguments

S

The penalty Hessian, a p x p symmetric matrix, dense or sparse. Matrix::isDiagonal() decides which route is taken, so a matrix stored as diagonal and one that only has zero off-diagonal entries are both treated as diagonal.

Value

A matrix with ncol(S) columns and one row per retained eigendirection, so at most p rows and fewer where the penalty has a null space. The result is a Matrix sparse matrix only where S is a diagonal matrix stored sparse; for any other S, including the zero matrix, it is a dense base matrix. NULL when the penalty is indefinite beyond the tolerance.

Why an eigendecomposition

A penalty is positive semidefinite and is often rank deficient. A spline's is deficient by exactly the dimension of its null space, the set of coefficient directions that the penalty does not shrink. A Cholesky factorization fails there, so the factor comes from an eigendecomposition with the non-positive eigenvalues dropped, and the rows that they would have contributed are absent. A zero matrix gives a factor with no rows.

A non-convex penalty has an indefinite Hessian and no such factor. NULL is returned and the caller falls back to the assembled route.

The diagonal shortcut

A diagonal penalty is factored by taking the square root of its diagonal. That is the same answer the eigendecomposition gives, since the eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, so the two routes agree by construction and a test pins them together.

The case is common. A ridge penalty and the penalty of a random effect with independent coefficients are diagonal, and so is the penalty of a smoother in the Demmler-Reinsch basis (see modelterms7::s()), which is zero on the null-space coordinates and a multiple of the smoothing parameter elsewhere. Any block-diagonal assembly of such penalties is diagonal as well. The factor is recomputed at every iteration of the scoring loop, so the diagonal route avoids one dense eigendecomposition per iteration.

See also

diagonal_sqrt() for the diagonal route, augmented_solve() for the solve this feeds, sqrt_design() for the other half of the augmented matrix.
